analysis.investment_thesis: Aditya Vision is a classic Lynch fast-grower — a dominant consumer electronics retailer in underpenetrated Bihar/Eastern India expanding its store footprint at 36%+ CAGR — but persistently negative and worsening free cash flow (-₹78 Cr in FY25 vs +₹13 Cr in FY22) means the growth engine is burning investor capital, not generating it. At a trailing PEG of ~1.4 (P/E 61.37 / 44% EPS CAGR), the story is good but the price is not cheap enough to absorb execution risk.
key_strengths: Exceptional 36% revenue CAGR (FY22→FY25) with net profit growing even faster at 44% CAGR — the story is working
ROCE of ~30% signals genuine capital efficiency in existing stores; the unit economics are sound
First-mover dominance in Bihar/Eastern India — underpenetrated Tier 2/3 market with long consumer durables adoption runway
key_risks: Operating cash flow has collapsed from +₹32 Cr (FY22) to -₹41 Cr (FY25) — growth is being funded by debt and equity raises, not operations
Total debt nearly doubled from ₹282 Cr to ₹480 Cr in 3 years; D/E at 0.65 and climbing — thin 6.57% margins leave no cushion if credit tightens
Specialty retail is a low-margin, inventory-heavy model: any economic slowdown, consumer sentiment softening, or competition from Croma/Reliance Digital could compress margins further
red_flags: FCF deteriorating every year: +13 → -13 → -41 → -78 Cr — the growth machine has never self-funded
OCF positive only 2 of last 4 years; the company is not cash-generative at current scale despite ₹2,260 Cr revenue
Financing CF consistently positive (raised ₹94 Cr in FY25) — growth is dependent on continuous external capital
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aditya Vision ticks many Lynch fast-grower boxes: a simple retail concept (consumer electronics) expanding store-by-store into a huge, underserved geography (Bihar has 120M+ people with low appliance penetration). Revenue has compounded at 36% for three straight years, profits at 44%, and ROCE at 30% tells you the existing stores are genuinely profitable. The forward PEG of ~0.95 (forward P/E 41.69 / ~44% growth) is borderline attractive for a quality fast-grower. I can walk into Patna and see these stores — that's exactly the kind of ground-level insight Lynch prizes.

But the cash flow statement kills the excitement. A retailer at ₹2,260 Cr in revenue should be generating operating cash, not burning ₹41 Cr of it. The culprit is working capital — rapid store expansion means inventory pileup and supplier credit strain. Debt has ballooned from ₹282 Cr to ₹480 Cr while FCF hit -₹78 Cr in FY25. Lynch loved growth, but he hated debt-fueled, cash-burning expansion in thin-margin businesses. Until AVL demonstrates the ability to fund its own growth — ideally OCF turning sustainably positive — this story is incomplete. Watch for FY26 OCF inflection before adding aggressively.
